'''Brian Gregory Keating''' (born September 9, 1971) is an American [[cosmologist]]. He works on observations of the [[cosmic microwave background]], leading the [[POLARBEAR]]2 and [[Simons Array]] experiments. He also conceived the first [[BICEP and Keck Array|BICEP]] experiment. He received his PhD in 2000, and is a distinguished professor of physics at [[University of California, San Diego]], since 2019. He is the author of two books, ''Losing The Nobel Prize'' and ''Into the Impossible''.

==Education and career==
Keating received his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] degree in [[physics]] at [[Case Western Reserve University]] in 1993.<ref name="simons" /><ref name="CV" /> He then obtained his [[Master of Science|M.S.]] and [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in physics at [[Brown University]].<ref name="CV" /> His thesis, titled ''A search for the large angular scale polarization of the cosmic microwave background'' and supervised by [[Peter Timbie]], was accepted in 2000.<ref name="thesis" /> He started as a [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) [[postdoctoral fellow]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 2001<ref name="nsf_fellow" /> until 2004. He was an assistant professor at the [[University of California, San Diego]] from 2004, before being promoted to associate professor there in 2009.<ref name="CV" /> He received an [[National Science Foundation CAREER Awards|NSF career grant]] in 2005, and a [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers|Presidential Early Career Award]] in 2006.<ref name="nsfaward2006" /> Keating was one of three scientists, along with [[Jonathan Kaufman (scientist)|Jonathan Kaufman]] and [[Bradley Johnson (scientist)|Bradley Johnson]], to receive the [[Buchalter Cosmology Prize]] in 2014.<ref name="CosmologyPrize" /> He became co-director of the [[Ax Center for Experimental Cosmology]] and the [[Joan & Irwin Jacobs Program in Astrophysics]] in 2013.<ref name="CV" />

Keating became a professor at UC San Diego in 2014.<ref name="CV" /> He became a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2016.<ref name="UCSD" /><ref name="APSfellow" /> In 2019 he became the Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics at UC San Diego,<ref name="UCSD" /><ref name="EndowedChairs" /> in the Center for Astrophysics & Space Sciences,<ref name="physicspage" /> which is part of the Department of Physics.<ref name="faculty" /> Keating received an Excellence in Stewardship Award in 2018/19, and is an honorary member of the [[National Society of Black Physicists]].<ref name="RocketMan" /> He is co-director of the [[Arthur C. Clarke Center for the Human Imagination]] at UC San Diego.<ref name="Wired2020" /> He received the [[Horace Mann]] Medal from [[Brown University Graduate School]] in 2022.<ref name="horacemann" />

== Research ==
Keating researches cosmology, focusing on the study of the cosmic microwave background and its relationship to the origin and evolution of the universe.<ref name="Nature2018" /> He conceived the [[BICEP and Keck Array|BICEP (Background Imaging of Cosmic Extragalactic Polarization)]] instrument, which observed from the [[South Pole]].<ref name="Astronomy2018" /> BICEP received a [[NASA Group Achievement Award]] in 2010.<ref name="NASAaward" /> In 2016 he convinced the [[Simons Foundation]] to provide US$38.4m of funding for what later became the Simons Array,<ref name="SanDiego2017" /> and in 2019 a US$20m grant from the Simons Foundation led to the creation of the [[Simons Observatory]],<ref name="Princeton2019" /> followed by an additional US$4.6m in 2021.<ref name="SanDiego2021" /> Keating co-leads POLARBEAR2 and the Simons Array in Chile,<ref name="RocketMan" /> is the Principal Investigator of Simons Observatory,<ref name="simonsfoundation2024" /> and has raised around US$100m of funding for CMB telescopes.<ref name="SD_2022" /> 

He has two patents, on a "wide-bandwidth polarization modulator for microwave and mm-wavelengths" in 2009,<ref name="polmodulator_patent" /> and "Tunnel junction fabrication" in 2016.<ref name="tunnel_patent" />

==Podcast and outreach==
[[File:Brian Keating at the Royal Institution 2023 10.jpg|thumb|Keating presenting at the [[Royal Institution]] in 2023<ref>{{cite AV media|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xKfWuRJFH7Y|people=Brian Keating|title=Charting the evolution of the universe|year=2023}}</ref>]]
Keating has hosted the Clarke Center ''Into the Impossible'' podcast since 2016.<ref name="CV" /> It takes its name from the second of [[Clarke's three laws]]: "The only way of discovering the limits of the possible is to venture a little way past them ''into the impossible''." Each episode is a long-form conversation with [[Nobel Laureate|nobel laureates]], scientists, writers and other notable individuals such as [[Stephen C. Meyer]] (an advocate of intelligent design<ref>{{cite web|url=https://drbriankeating.medium.com/a-conversation-prof-adb9d71fca22|title=A conversation: Prof. Brian Keating with Dr. Steven Meyer, author of Darwin's Doubt and Return of the God Hypothesis|first=Brian|last=Keating|publisher=Medium|date=2021-04-21|accessdate=2024-03-26}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://podcasts.apple.com/no/podcast/stephen-meyer-return-of-the-god-hypothesis/id1169885840?i=1000515021472&l=nb|title=Stephen Meyer: Return of the God Hypothesis|publisher=Apple|accessdate=2024-03-26}}</ref>), [[Noam Chomsky]], [[Eric Weinstein]], [[Jill Tarter]], [[Sara Seager]]<ref name="Wired2020" /> lasting around an hour. {{As of|2022}} it has hosted 11 Nobel Prize winners and two recipients of the [[Pulitzer Prize]].<ref name="SD_2022" /> It reached 200,000 subscribers in 2024.<ref>{{cite AV media|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aBNgnk2RqrY|title=Celebrating 200k subscribers|people=Brian Keating|year=2024}}</ref>

Keating also appeared in {{ill|The Michael Shermer Show|qid=Q109650493|short=1}} podcast in 2019,<ref name="Shermer2019" /> and the [[Lex Fridman Podcast]] in 2022.<ref name="fridman2022" /> He has also recorded videos for [[Conservatism_in_the_United_States|conservative]] website [[PragerU]],<ref name="PragerU"/> and has talked about popular science connected with [[The Witcher (TV series)|The Witcher]] television series.<ref name="Witcher" /> He appeared in the "Mysteries Of The Moon" episode of [[The UnXplained]].<ref name="UnXplained" />

He also teaches astronomy to high school students since 2012 as part of his outreach work,<ref name="RocketMan" /><ref name="CV" /> and has given presentations to over 3,000 K-12 students since 1994.<ref name="CV" />

He has also co-narrated a 21-hour audio book of [[Galileo Galilei]]'s ''[[Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems]]'' in 2022.<ref name="dialogue" />

== Books about the Nobel Prize ==
Keating is critical of the way that Nobel Prizes are organized, saying that "No scientist arrives alone in Stockholm." He has written two books on the topic.<ref name="mundo" /> The Nobel Prize was a motivating factor in Keating's career due to his academic rivalry with his father.<ref name="SD_2021" />

===''Losing The Nobel Prize'' (2018)===
Keating published his first book ''Losing the Nobel Prize: A Story of Cosmology, Ambition, and the Perils of Science's Highest Honor'' on April 24, 2018.<ref name="Keating2018" /><ref name="Astronomy2018" /> The book describes the [[BICEP and Keck Array#BICEP1|BICEP]] and [[BICEP and Keck Array#BICEP2|BICEP2]] experiments, which were located at the South Pole and were devised to detect and map the polarization of the cosmic microwave background radiation leftover from the [[Big Bang]]. BICEP2's data showed strong polarization signals that were announced to be cosmological in origin, but were later shown by [[Planck (spacecraft)|Planck satellite]] data to be caused by polarized interstellar dust.

The first part of the book describes the background behind [[cosmological inflation]], and the second covers BICEP2. The third section focuses on Keating's issues with the Nobel Prize, including lack of diversity in the recipients, that the prize cannot be awarded posthumously,<ref name="Nature2018" /> the maximum of three laureates per prize, which excludes larger groups from receiving it,<ref name="Science2018" /> and the secrecy around nominations. According to Keating, all of these "reward an outdated version of science",<ref name="Guardian2019" /> and "better science comes from inclusivity, collaboration, and innovation".<ref name="Astronomy2018" /> He argues that the science Nobel Prizes have strayed from the original intent of [[Alfred Nobel]]'s will, and may hinder scientific progress by fostering unnecessary, and sometimes destructive, competition.<ref name="Nature2019" /> He proposed that half a Nobel prize should go to the leaders of a collaboration, with the other half awarded to the rest of the team of scientists working on the project.<ref name="Space2018" />

=== ''Into the Impossible'' (2021) ===
His second book, ''Into the Impossible'', was published in 2021.<ref name="podcast_impossible" /> It features interviews with Nobel Prize winners [[Adam Riess]], [[Rainer Weiss]], [[Sheldon Glashow]], [[Carl Wieman]], [[Roger Penrose]], [[Duncan Haldane]], [[Frank Wilczek]], [[John C. Mather]] and [[Barry Barish]].<ref name="Keating2021" />
== Personal life ==
Keating was born on September 9, 1971,<ref name="podcast_impossible" /> the son of the mathematician [[James Ax]],<ref name="Quanta2020" /> and his wife Barbara.<ref name="Keating2018" /> When he was about seven, his parents divorced and his mother remarried, and the young Brian took his stepfather's name, Keating. He was out of contact with his father for the next 15 years, reconnecting only when he was a graduate student. Keating grew up in [[Dobbs Ferry]], New York.<ref name="Keating2018" /> He has three brothers: Kevin, Nick and Shaya.<ref name="Quanta2020" /> 

Keating was born to [[Jewish]] parents, but they divorced and his mother married a Catholic. He became a member of the [[Catholic Church]], although his mother and [[father]] were non-observant Jews. He later became an [[atheist]], and subsequently he became an observant Jew, currently describing himself as a "practicing devout agnostic".<ref name="Quanta2020" />

As well as a cosmologist, he is a pilot with a multi-engine turbine license.<ref name="simons" /> He was a trustee of [[Math for America, San Diego]] in 2006–2014, [[Angel Flight West]] in 2010–2015, and the [[National Museum of Mathematics]] in 2014–2017. He is currently a trustee of [[San Diego Air & Space Museum]] since 2013, and is on the [[Ruben H. Fleet Museum]] advisory council since 2017.<ref name="CV" />
